Q011870:
## Why the data size decides
Single-node libraries such as scikit-learn load the whole training matrix into the memory of one machine (on Databricks, the driver). Databricks recommends keeping training on one machine when possible, because distributed code is more complex and slower from communication overhead, but says to consider distributed training when the data or model is too large to fit in memory on a single machine.
## What Spark ML adds
Spark ML (`pyspark.ml`, the DataFrame-based MLlib API) runs each algorithm as Spark jobs: rows stay in partitions on the workers, and each iteration aggregates partial results (for example gradients) instead of collecting the data. Adding workers adds memory and compute. The same `Pipeline` also runs where the data already lives, so there is no copy to the driver.
- Choose Spark ML when the training data cannot fit on one node, when the features are produced by Spark transformations on a big table, or when scoring happens inside Spark jobs.
- Choose a single node (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch) when the data fits comfortably and you need an algorithm or accuracy that Spark ML does not offer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Swap space:** paging a training matrix from disk makes each pass over the data orders of magnitude slower and is not a supported way to extend memory; it does not give a usable nightly job.
- ✗ **B. 0.1% sample:** a sample can be a valid choice when a learning curve is flat, but here the requirement explicitly needs the full history and rare segments, and a 0.1% sample would drop them.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** A Spark ML pipeline is the design that scales with the data. The 1.2 billion rows never leave the workers, the logistic regression is trained by the distributed solver, and the fitted `PipelineModel` can score on the same cluster.
- ✗ **D. toPandas on the driver:** `toPandas()` collects every row to the driver process, so it fails with out-of-memory exactly because the data is larger than the largest node.

## Key idea
When the training data does not fit on one node, use a distributed library such as Spark ML; otherwise stay on a single node.
Q011871:
## Fit the tool to the data and the algorithm
The 3 GB table fits easily in memory on one node. Distributed training pays communication and scheduling costs in every iteration, so for data this small a single node is usually faster and simpler. A model that already beats the Spark ML alternatives is a second reason to keep it.
## A common split of work
- Use Spark for what it is good at: reading, joining and aggregating the large source tables into a feature table.
- Convert the finished feature table to pandas (`toPandas()` or the Spark-to-pandas Arrow path) and train on a single node with the library the team trusts.
- Revisit Spark ML or another distributed option (Ray, TorchDistributor for neural networks) only when the data or model no longer fits on one machine.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Linear regression only:** Spark ML has many families (trees, ensembles, GBT, ALS, KMeans); the claim is false, and switching to a linear model would likely lose accuracy.
- ✗ **B. Rewrite as GBTRegressor:** distributed training is not always faster. On 3 GB the per-iteration communication outweighs the gain, and the team has measured that Spark ML does not reach the same error.
- ✗ **C. Training inside mapInPandas:** `mapInPandas` runs a function on each partition independently, so each worker would train its own separate model on a slice; it does not combine them into one model.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Preparing features in Spark and training scikit-learn on a single node keeps the better algorithm, avoids distribution overhead on 3 GB, and leaves a clear trigger (data outgrowing memory) for moving to Spark ML.

## Key idea
When the data fits on one node and the single-node algorithm is better, use Spark for data preparation and train on a single node.
Q011872:
## Spark ML parallelism follows partitions
Spark ML algorithms run as ordinary Spark jobs: one task processes one partition of the training DataFrame, and the iterative or per-level aggregation happens across those tasks. If the DataFrame has 8 partitions, at most 8 cores work on each pass, however large the cluster is.
## What to check
- Compare the number of tasks in the Spark UI stage with the total executor cores.
- Repartition to a small multiple of the core count (`df.repartition(320)`) so all cores get work and one slow partition does not dominate.
- Cache the repartitioned DataFrame when the algorithm makes many passes (random forest levels, logistic regression iterations), so the shuffle is paid once.
- Adding workers to a job with too few partitions only adds idle cores.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Move to scikit-learn:** the number of files only limits the initial partition count and is cheap to change; a single driver gives up the distribution that the data size may need.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Spark ML tasks follow the partitions of the input. Repartitioning to a multiple of the cores spreads the passes over the whole cluster, and caching pays the shuffle once for all passes.
- ✗ **C. Driver memory:** the tasks run on executors and the idle cores are caused by too few partitions, not by driver memory.
- ✗ **D. More trees:** trees are built level by level over the partitions, not one task per tree, so the number of trees does not create tasks.

## Key idea
Spark ML uses as many cores as the DataFrame has partitions; repartition to a multiple of the cores and cache before fit.
Q011873:
## Use the learning curve
A learning curve plots validation error against training-set size. When the curve is flat, extra rows add cost without adding accuracy. Training on a representative sample on one node can then give the same quality at a fraction of the cost, and lets the team use an algorithm that is only available as a single-node library.
## Conditions for this trade-off
- The sample must be representative (stratified on the label or key segments if they are rare).
- The learning curve must be re-checked when the data or the problem changes, because the plateau can move.
- If rare segments need the full history, or the curve is still falling, Spark ML (or another distributed option) on the full table is justified.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A sample past the plateau keeps accuracy, cuts compute from hours of cluster time to a single node, and lets the team keep XGBoost. Re-running the learning curve guards against distribution change.
- ✗ **B. 24 monthly models averaged:** this changes the problem (each model sees one month and misses seasonal or cross-month patterns) and the averaged ensemble is not a drop-in for the original model.
- ✗ **C. Add workers:** scaling out reduces wall-clock time but not cost per unit of accuracy, and it does not address that the extra data is not improving the model.
- ✗ **D. Train on all 1 TB:** the curve shows more rows do not lower validation error here, so the cost buys nothing and the team gives up its tuned model.

## Key idea
A flat learning curve means a representative sample on one node can match full-data distributed training at far lower cost.
Q011874:
## Where single-node libraries run
Libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost (single-node) and PyTorch on one device execute in the Python process where the code is called, which is the driver of a Databricks cluster. Spark does not distribute them automatically. A cluster with workers helps only if the code uses Spark APIs (Spark ML, Spark SQL, pandas function APIs) or a distributed framework (Ray, TorchDistributor, `joblibspark` for parallel trials).
## Options for using more machines
- Use one bigger single node when the data fits, since the fit then uses all of its cores.
- Switch to Spark ML (or a distributed variant of the algorithm) when the data no longer fits.
- Parallelize independent trials or per-group models, not one model fit, with pandas function APIs, Ray or Optuna on Spark.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Repartitioning:** partition count affects Spark jobs, but the scikit-learn fit does not run on Spark partitions at all, so repartitioning does not move the work.
- ✗ **B. n_jobs per executor:** `n_jobs` sets processes or threads inside the one Python process, not executors, and restarting executors changes nothing.
- ✗ **C. Config flag:** there is no such Spark setting; workers are already part of the cluster, they just are not used by non-Spark code.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The fit is plain scikit-learn in the driver process, so extra workers sit idle. Choose a bigger single node, a distributed algorithm, or parallelize many independent fits.

## Key idea
Single-node libraries run on the driver only; extra workers help only with Spark or distributed frameworks.
Q011875:
## Distribution has overhead
A distributed algorithm splits rows over workers, computes partial results, and combines them over the network at every iteration or tree level. Scheduling tasks and moving partial results costs time that does not shrink with more workers. If one node holds the data and has enough cores, the single-node library avoids these costs.
## When the picture changes
- When data no longer fits in the memory of one node, single node is not an option and Spark ML scales better.
- When the number of rows or features grows large, the compute per iteration grows and the fixed overhead becomes small in comparison.
- A cluster-size increase helps only when per-task work, not overhead, is the bottleneck.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** With 5 GB the compute is small and the overhead of the distributed algorithm dominates, so the single node wins. Spark ML pays off when the data outgrows one machine.
- ✗ **B. More workers:** adding workers increases coordination, and for small data it can make the run slower rather than faster.
- ✗ **C. Driver-only trees:** Spark ML tree algorithms distribute the work to executors, which is why they scale to large data.
- ✗ **D. Always slower:** it is not true at every size. Past the memory limit of a single node, scikit-learn cannot run at all and Spark ML wins.

## Key idea
For data that fits on one node, distribution overhead makes a single node faster; Spark ML pays off beyond the memory of one machine.
Q011876:
## Missing values are learned state
`Imputer` is an `Estimator`. `fit` computes a surrogate value per column (mean by default, or median or mode) and returns an `ImputerModel` that stores them. All `null` and `NaN` values in the input columns are treated as missing and replaced. The input columns must be numeric.
## Why it belongs in the pipeline
- The fill values come from the training data and travel inside the saved `PipelineModel`, so scoring uses the same numbers without any copy.
- Median is robust to outliers, which matters for skewed columns such as income.
- Dropping rows (skip) changes the population: new customers with few records are lost, and a scoring job would silently return fewer predictions than it received.
- Imputers do not handle categorical features well: encode those with `StringIndexer` first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. fillna(0) in notebooks:** a constant of 0 is a modelling choice that distorts income, and the call has to be repeated by hand in every scoring job, where the copies drift.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The `Imputer` stage learns the medians at `fit` and keeps them in the `PipelineModel`, so every training and scoring batch gets the same fill values and no row is removed.
- ✗ **C. Hand-written SQL:** the training means are copied into every consumer, which is the training-serving mismatch that a stored `ImputerModel` avoids, and a mean is not robust to outliers.
- ✗ **D. Skipping rows:** invalid rows are removed, so the model never sees the new customers and scoring returns fewer rows than requested, which breaks joins on the output.

## Key idea
Use an Imputer stage so that the fill values are learned once and stored in the PipelineModel.
Q011877:
## Keep feature logic inside the pipeline
Anything computed outside the pipeline must be repeated by hand at scoring, and the two copies drift. Spark ML offers stateless `Transformer` stages for row-level logic. `SQLTransformer` runs a SQL statement in which `__THIS__` stands for the input DataFrame, so a derived column becomes a stage of the `Pipeline`. It is saved and loaded with the `PipelineModel`.
## Rules of thumb
- Row-level derived columns (ratios, flags, date parts): `SQLTransformer`.
- Anything that has to learn from the data (scaling, indexing, imputing): an Estimator stage whose fitted state is stored in the model.
- With ANSI mode on (the default in Spark 4), `clicks / impressions` raises an error when `impressions` is 0: write `try_divide(clicks, impressions)` in the stage to get NULL instead.
- Logic that cannot be expressed in a stage belongs in a documented, versioned feature pipeline, not in an ad hoc notebook cell.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nightly job on the raw table:** this adds a second pipeline that must stay in step with the model, and the column stays absent for any source that is not that table.
- ✗ **B. Documenting the formula:** it relies on every consumer to reimplement it exactly, which is the training-serving mismatch the artifact is meant to avoid.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The `SQLTransformer` stage makes `ctr` part of the saved `PipelineModel`, so training and scoring run the same formula from the same artifact.
- ✗ **D. Scoring-side UDF:** it duplicates the logic in a second place and can differ in null and division-by-zero handling from the notebook version.

## Key idea
Put row-level feature logic in the pipeline (SQLTransformer) so the saved PipelineModel reproduces it.
Q011878:
## Centering makes sparse data dense
`StandardScaler` has `withMean` set to false by default; centering subtracts the mean from every entry, so a sparse vector becomes dense. The Spark documentation warns that this builds a dense output. With 8 million dimensions per row, the dense output cannot be held in memory.
## Scalers that keep sparsity
- `MaxAbsScaler` rescales each feature to [-1, 1] by dividing through its maximum absolute value. It does not shift or center the data, and so it does not destroy any sparsity.
- `StandardScaler` with the default `withMean=False` scales to unit standard deviation only and also keeps sparse vectors sparse.
- `MinMaxScaler` subtracts the minimum, and `RobustScaler(withCentering=True)` subtracts the median, so both can make sparse vectors dense.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More memory for centering:** dense vectors of 8 million values per row are far beyond any realistic executor size, and the shift is not required to make the features comparable in scale.
- ✗ **B. MinMaxScaler:** it subtracts each feature's minimum before scaling, and any non-zero minimum turns zeros into non-zero values, which makes the vectors dense.
- ✗ **C. RobustScaler with centering:** removing the median is also a shift, and the documentation warns that centering builds a dense output.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `MaxAbsScaler` only divides, so zero entries stay zero and the vectors stay sparse. It is an `Estimator`, so the maxima learned at `fit` are stored in the pipeline.

## Key idea
For high-dimensional sparse features, scale with MaxAbsScaler or StandardScaler without centering.
Q011879:
## Vector size in metadata
`VectorAssembler` needs the size of every input vector column to build output metadata. For a batch DataFrame, Spark can inspect the contents. In a streaming DataFrame, the contents are not available until the stream starts, so the size must come from column metadata.
## VectorSizeHint
`VectorSizeHint` is a transformer with `inputCol` and `size`. It adds the vector size to the column metadata so `VectorAssembler` and other stages can use that column. Its optional `handleInvalid` parameter controls vectors with nulls or the wrong size: `error` (default), `skip` (filter those rows) or `optimistic` (do not check, and so the metadata can disagree with the content).
- Put it directly before the stage that needs the size.
- Use `error` or `skip` rather than `optimistic` unless the producer is fully trusted.
- Fitting estimators still needs batch data: apply the fitted model to the stream with `transform`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** `VectorSizeHint` writes the known size of `emb` into the column metadata, so `VectorAssembler` can run on a streaming DataFrame without looking at the data.
- ✗ **B. VectorSlicer:** it selects entries by index and still depends on knowing the input vector, it does not declare the size of the column in the metadata.
- ✗ **C. Normalizer:** it rescales each vector to unit norm and leaves the column metadata without a declared vector length.
- ✗ **D. cache on a stream:** streaming DataFrames cannot be cached for batch inspection, and the contents appear only after the query starts.

## Key idea
Put VectorSizeHint before VectorAssembler when vector columns come from a streaming DataFrame.
Q011880:
## A Pipeline is an Estimator
A `Pipeline` has `fit` and returns a `PipelineModel`, so it is an `Estimator` and can be a stage in another `Pipeline`. The outer `fit` fits the nested pipeline (producing a nested `PipelineModel`) and passes its output to the later stages.
## Why this helps
- The shared featurization is defined in one place and versioned once.
- Each model pipeline is `Pipeline(stages=[featurization, classifier])`, so the saved outer `PipelineModel` is a single artifact that scores raw columns.
- Tuning with `CrossValidator` still re-fits the nested stages per fold, as needed to avoid leakage.
## When to separate
If many models must use the same fitted encodings (for instance, identical index values), fit the featurization once, save the `PipelineModel`, and reuse it as a transformer stage; accept that tuning then does not refit it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Collect and rebuild:** `collect()` moves the data to the driver, and rebuilding pipelines from rows throws away the fitted stage state and does not scale.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Using the featurization `Pipeline` as the first stage of each model pipeline keeps one definition and gives a self-contained artifact per model.
- ✗ **C. Fitted PipelineModel in the stage list:** a fitted `PipelineModel` is a `Transformer` and can be placed as a stage, but then it is fixed to the training data of the first fit, and the option as written replaces rather than reuses the definition.
- ✗ **D. Three stage copies:** sharing a stage definition is exactly what nesting a pipeline provides; copying objects gives three diverging definitions, and the claim about single-use is not a rule.

## Key idea
A Pipeline is an Estimator, so a shared featurization Pipeline can be the first stage of many model pipelines.
Q011881:
## Indices are learned state
`StringIndexer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` computes a mapping from category to index (by default ordered by frequency, most frequent first). When the data changes, frequencies and categories change, so the next `fit` can assign different numbers to the same category. A model trained on the old numbers then receives indices with a different meaning.
## Design consequences
- Treat indexed values as private to the fitted model, not as shared data. Store raw values and let each model's `PipelineModel` map them at scoring time.
- Alphabetical ordering makes the order deterministic for a fixed set of categories, but a new category still shifts alphabetical positions of the ones after it.
- If an indexed column must be shared, fit the indexer once, version the fitted model, and reuse it without refitting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. maxCategories:** that is a `VectorIndexer` parameter for deciding which vector features are categorical, not a stability setting for `StringIndexer`.
- ✗ **B. Fit on a 10% sample:** the mapping depends on the content of the data used, not on the sample size, and a sample would miss rare categories too.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The index mapping is part of each model's learned state. Keeping the raw category in the table, and mapping through the pipeline that the model was trained with, removes the dependence on refit order.
- ✗ **D. Alphabetical ordering:** it removes the frequency-based reordering, but any new category inserts a new index and shifts later ones, so old consumers can still break.

## Key idea
Index mappings are learned model state; share raw values and apply each model's own fitted pipeline.
Q011882:
## Labels must be numeric
Spark ML classifiers require a numeric label column of indices 0 to numClasses-1. A `StringIndexer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` learns the mapping from strings to indices (ordered by frequency by default) and returns a `StringIndexerModel`.
## Getting strings back
`IndexToString` is a `Transformer` that converts indices to the original labels, using either the metadata attached to the column by the indexer or an explicit `labels` list. Place it after the classifier, with `inputCol="prediction"`, and it appends the readable label. Because the mapping is stored in the fitted pipeline, the strings in the report always match the indices the model used.
- Use `StringIndexer` for labels and also for categorical features (before `OneHotEncoder` when needed).
- Never recreate the mapping by hand: any difference from the model's mapping silently mislabels predictions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bucketizer:** it bins numeric values with fixed splits; it cannot read strings, and a hand dictionary again leaves the mapping outside the pipeline.
- ✗ **B. Cast to int:** casting non-numeric strings gives null, so the label would be lost.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The indexer learns the label mapping during `fit`, and `IndexToString` reverses it from the stored labels, so the whole path is inside the pipeline.
- ✗ **D. OneHotEncoder on the label:** Spark ML classifiers expect a single numeric index column as label, not a vector of dummy columns.

## Key idea
Use StringIndexer for string labels and IndexToString to turn predictions back into the original text.
Q011883:
## Estimator that learns, Transformer that applies
`Bucketizer` is a `Transformer`: you give it explicit `splits` and it maps values to bucket indices. `QuantileDiscretizer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` computes approximate quantiles of the input column and returns a `Bucketizer` model with those splits. The number of buckets can be smaller than requested if the input has too few distinct values.
## Why it matters for scoring
The splits are learned once from the training data and stored in the fitted `PipelineModel`. New batches are binned with the same boundaries, so a customer of a given age always lands in the same bin, and the model's learned coefficients stay valid.
- Use `Bucketizer` when the business defines the boundaries.
- Use `QuantileDiscretizer` when equal-frequency bins should be learned from training data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Repeated Binarizer:** `Binarizer` thresholds a value to 0/1 and thresholds are fixed numbers you must choose, so it does not learn quantiles and gives overlapping indicators rather than one bin.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** `QuantileDiscretizer` learns equal-frequency boundaries from the training data and freezes them in a `Bucketizer`, which the pipeline applies unchanged to later batches.
- ✗ **C. StandardScaler:** it centers and scales values; it does not bin, and z-scores are not equal-frequency groups.
- ✗ **D. Splits per scoring batch:** boundaries recomputed on each batch change the meaning of every bin between batches and break the model's learned weights.

## Key idea
QuantileDiscretizer (an Estimator) learns equal-frequency splits and keeps them as a Bucketizer; Bucketizer alone applies fixed splits.
Q011884:
## Two ways to build term-frequency vectors
- `HashingTF` is a `Transformer` that hashes each term into one of `numFeatures` buckets (default 2^18). It needs no global dictionary, which is cheap for huge corpora, but different words can share a bucket (collisions) and the word-to-position mapping is not stored.
- `CountVectorizer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` builds a vocabulary (limited by `vocabSize` and by document-frequency thresholds such as `minDF`) and the resulting model keeps `vocabulary`, so position i can be mapped back to a word.
## Trade-off
Hashing scales without a vocabulary pass and has fixed memory, but weights cannot be reliably named. If model explanations by word are required, use `CountVectorizer` and cap the vocabulary so that the vector size stays manageable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Only `CountVectorizer` keeps the term list, so coefficients of the logistic regression can be matched to words; capping `vocabSize` and `minDF` handles the huge number of terms.
- ✗ **B. HashingTF with 2^10 buckets:** hashing never stores the words, and so few buckets cause heavy collisions that merge unrelated terms.
- ✗ **C. HashingTF with a huge size:** more buckets reduce collisions but cannot invert a hash; several words can still map to one index and the word is not recoverable.
- ✗ **D. IDF keeps names:** `IDF` learns inverse document frequencies per vector position; it holds no vocabulary, so it cannot name positions.

## Key idea
Use CountVectorizer when you must map weights back to words; HashingTF is stateless and cheap but not reversible.
Q011885:
## Cold start in ALS
`ALS` learns a latent factor vector for each user and item seen in training. A user or item that appears only in the validation data has no factors, so `transform` returns `NaN` for those rows. By default (`coldStartStrategy="nan"`) the NaN stays in the predictions, so an evaluator averaging them returns `NaN` and model selection becomes impossible.
## The documented remedy
Setting `coldStartStrategy="drop"` drops prediction rows with NaN, so the metric is computed on the remaining rows only.
- Report the share of dropped rows, because dropping makes the metric optimistic when many users are new.
- For production cold start, combine ALS with a popularity or content-based fallback; ALS alone cannot rank unseen users.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. rank 200:** a larger rank adds capacity for known users and items, but unseen ones still have no factor vector.
- ✗ **B. nonnegative:** it constrains factors to be non-negative; it does not create factors for unknown users.
- ✗ **C. mae:** any metric computed over NaN predictions is NaN; the metric name is not the cause.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** With `coldStartStrategy="drop"` the NaN predictions for unseen users and items are removed, so RMSE is computed on the rest and the cross-validation can pick a model.

## Key idea
Use coldStartStrategy="drop" for ALS evaluation, and watch how many rows are dropped.
Q011886:
## KMeans uses distances
KMeans assigns each point to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance. A feature with a numeric range of hundreds of thousands dominates the distance, so the clusters reflect it and ignore a feature with range 0 to 30.
## Scale first
`StandardScaler` is an `Estimator` that learns each feature's mean and standard deviation (`withStd` is true by default, `withMean` is false by default, because centering a sparse vector makes it dense) and produces a `StandardScalerModel`. Put it between `VectorAssembler` and `KMeans` in the pipeline, and its learned statistics are reused when new customers are assigned to clusters.
- Evaluate with `ClusteringEvaluator` (silhouette score) and compare values of k.
- Tree-based models are insensitive to scale; distance-based models (KMeans, KNN, regularized linear models) are not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. LogisticRegression:** it is a supervised classifier, and there are no labels in this clustering task.
- ✗ **B. More iterations:** KMeans converges to a local optimum under the same distance; more iterations do not change the weighting of features.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Standardizing puts both features on a comparable scale, so the distance reflects both and the visit pattern can shape the clusters.
- ✗ **D. Larger k:** more clusters subdivide the income axis further; the unscaled distance still ignores the small-range feature.

## Key idea
Scale features before distance-based algorithms such as KMeans.
Q011887:
## Selectors in Spark ML
- `UnivariateFeatureSelector` picks a score function from the types you set: categorical features with a categorical label use chi-squared; continuous features with a categorical label use the ANOVA F-test; continuous features with a continuous label use the F-value (regression). Selection modes include `numTopFeatures`, `percentile` and `fpr`. It is an `Estimator`: it learns which feature indices to keep.
- `ChiSqSelector` is the older chi-squared selector for categorical features.
- `VarianceThresholdSelector` removes low-variance features without using the label.
- `PCA` creates new combined components, not a subset of the original features.
## Pipeline placement
Put the selector after `VectorAssembler` and fit it inside the cross-validated pipeline, because it uses the label and can leak validation information if fitted on the whole set.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. PCA:** PCA outputs 200 new components that mix features, not the 200 most associated original features, and it does not use the label.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Continuous features with a categorical label call for the ANOVA F-test, which `UnivariateFeatureSelector` applies with `numTopFeatures=200`.
- ✗ **C. ChiSqSelector for continuous features:** chi-squared expects categorical features, and its statistic is not a correlation.
- ✗ **D. VarianceThresholdSelector:** it ignores the label and keeps features by variance, so it does not measure association with the 4 classes.

## Key idea
For continuous features with a categorical label, use UnivariateFeatureSelector (ANOVA) inside the cross-validated pipeline.
Q011888:
## Random folds leak groups
`CrossValidator` splits rows at random. If one customer's transactions are spread over the folds, the model sees that customer in training and is then validated on the same customer, memorizing customer-specific patterns. Scores are optimistic for new customers, which is the production situation.
## foldCol
`CrossValidator` accepts `foldCol`, a column with user-specified fold numbers. Spark then skips random k-fold and uses your assignment. The column must be an integer in the range 0 to numFolds-1; out-of-range values raise an error. Assigning folds by a hash of the group key keeps all rows of a customer in the same fold.
- Make the fold assignment deterministic and independent of the label.
- Check fold sizes: very uneven groups give uneven folds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** `foldCol` with a customer-based fold number makes every customer appear in only one validation fold, so the score measures performance on unseen customers.
- ✗ **B. Fixed seed:** a seed makes the random folds repeatable but they stay random with respect to customers.
- ✗ **C. TrainValidationSplit:** it also splits rows at random into train and validation, so customers are still shared; it has no foldCol.
- ✗ **D. More folds:** the leakage comes from customers spread over folds, and smaller folds do not keep a customer together.

## Key idea
For grouped data, assign folds by group with foldCol so that no group is split across training and validation.
Q011889:
## What parallelism does
By default `CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` evaluate parameter settings in serial. `setParallelism(n)` with n of 2 or more fits n models concurrently. The Spark documentation advises choosing a value that maximizes parallelism without exceeding cluster resources, notes that larger values may not improve performance, and says a value up to 10 is generally sufficient.
## Interaction with a big fit
If each fit already uses the whole cluster, running more fits at once only shares the same cores and memory, so there is no gain and memory pressure increases (each concurrent fit caches its data and tree statistics).
- Raise parallelism when each fit is small compared with the cluster (small data, few partitions).
- Keep it at 1 to 2 when each fit is large.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Not allowed for trees:** parallelism is a general setting and works for any estimator; the problem is resource contention.
- ✗ **B. Only validation:** the parameter evaluates complete fit-and-evaluate runs for different parameter settings, which includes training.
- ✗ **C. Minimum of 64:** there is no minimum tied to workers times cores; the value is the number of concurrent model fits, and the documentation says up to 10 is generally enough.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Concurrent fits compete for the same executors and memory, so a large single fit leaves no spare capacity; a small value matches what the cluster can hold.

## Key idea
Parallelism is the number of concurrent fits; it helps only when each fit leaves spare cluster capacity.
Q011890:
## Tuning without labels
`CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` need an `Evaluator` whose metric tells which `ParamMap` is better. Classification and regression evaluators compare predictions with a label column, which an unsupervised task does not have. `ClusteringEvaluator` computes the silhouette score (by default with squared Euclidean distance) from the feature vectors and the cluster assignments only.
## Cautions
- The silhouette score is a larger-is-better measure, so no change of direction is needed.
- It is distance based: scale the features before `KMeans` and before evaluating, otherwise one feature decides the score.
- The score usually changes little between neighbouring values of `k`: also consider the business use and the cost of the cluster count.
- At 80 million rows, `TrainValidationSplit` fits each `k` once, while `CrossValidator` would multiply the cost by the number of folds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. f1 on random labels:** the metric would compare cluster numbers with noise, and cluster indices have no fixed meaning that could match any label.
- ✗ **B. RMSE on the cluster index:** the index is an arbitrary identifier, so a difference between two identifiers carries no information about fit.
- ✗ **C. BinaryClassificationEvaluator:** it needs a true label and a raw prediction column, and clusters are not positive and negative classes.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `ClusteringEvaluator` measures cluster separation without labels, so the grid over `k` can be scored and the best model chosen by the highest silhouette.

## Key idea
Tune unsupervised models with an evaluator that needs no label, such as ClusteringEvaluator.
Q011891:
## MLlib tuning takes a list of ParamMaps
`CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` need an `Estimator`, a list of `ParamMap`s (`estimatorParamMaps`) and an `Evaluator`. `ParamGridBuilder` builds the full Cartesian product of the lists given with `addGrid`. It has no random mode.
## Random search with MLlib
Since `estimatorParamMaps` is just a list, you can build it yourself: draw 40 combinations from your distributions and create one `ParamMap` per draw (a dict from estimator params to values). The evaluator and cross-validation logic stay the same.
- Random search often finds a good region with far fewer fits than a full grid when only a few hyperparameters matter.
- For adaptive search (Bayesian, early stopping), use a tuning library such as Optuna instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. numFolds=40:** `numFolds` sets how the data is split for validation, not how many parameter combinations are tried.
- ✗ **B. Distributions in addGrid:** `addGrid` takes a list of values, not a distribution object, and `CrossValidator` does no sampling.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Because `estimatorParamMaps` accepts any list of `ParamMap`s, 40 sampled combinations can be passed in directly and evaluated by the normal cross-validation.
- ✗ **D. setRandom:** the builder has no such method; it enumerates every combination of the values added.

## Key idea
MLlib has only grid generation; for random search, pass your own sampled list of ParamMaps.
Q011892:
## Time order must be respected
In forecasting, the model is used on dates after its training data. A random split lets the model train on rows from after a validation row, and neighboring days are strongly correlated, so validation rows have near duplicates in training. The score is then far better than the error on truly future data.
## What to do in Spark ML
Spark ML has no time-series cross-validation. Split by a timestamp: train on the earlier period and validate on the later one (and repeat over several cut-off dates if needed), then compare parameter maps on the later period. A hold-out final test on the newest period gives the estimate for deployment.
- Lag and rolling features must be computed using only earlier rows.
- `foldCol` can group rows into time blocks, but it still trains on blocks that are later than the validation block, so it is not a replacement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bigger grid:** more combinations do not remove leakage from the split and can overfit it further.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Splitting by time prevents the training data from containing the future of the validation rows, so the metric reflects forward-looking performance.
- ✗ **C. Shuffling more:** the random mixing is the problem; shuffling or using more folds adds more future rows to training.
- ✗ **D. Evaluator invalid:** `RegressionEvaluator` works on any numeric predictions; the issue is how the data was split.

## Key idea
For time-dependent data, validate on a later period than training; random folds leak the future.
Q011893:
## What avgMetrics contains
`CrossValidatorModel.avgMetrics` has one value per `ParamMap`: the metric averaged over the folds for that setting. The best value is the maximum of many noisy estimates, and the parameters were picked because of it, so it is optimistically biased as an estimate of the final quality.
## Honest estimate
- Split off a test set first (for instance with `randomSplit` and a seed, or by time).
- Run cross-validation on the training part only.
- Evaluate `cvModel.bestModel`, the `Pipeline` model refit on the whole training part with the best parameters, once on the test set.
The same applies to `TrainValidationSplit`. Training-set scores say nothing about generalization.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A test set untouched by tuning gives an unbiased estimate; `bestModel` is evaluated on it once and that figure goes in the model card.
- ✗ **B. Maximum is unbiased:** selecting the maximum over many candidates on the same folds is a form of selection bias, so it overstates quality.
- ✗ **C. Training score:** fitted models score best on data they have seen, so this gives the most optimistic number.
- ✗ **D. Average of avgMetrics:** the mean over all parameter maps mixes good and poor settings and describes no deployable model.

## Key idea
Report the score of the best model on a test set not used for tuning, not the best cross-validation metric.
Q011894:
## Why a distributed Optuna study needs shared storage
An Optuna `Study` is a record of trials: the parameters tried and the objective value returned. A sampler such as TPE reads that record to decide which parameters to try next. With the default in-memory storage the record lives inside one Python process. If 40 workers each create a study, there are 40 separate records and 40 separate searches that only look alike.
## The Databricks integration
The Databricks page "Hyperparameter tuning with Optuna" describes two classes from MLflow 3:
- `MlflowStorage` lets Optuna use the MLflow tracking server (one experiment) as its storage backend, so every worker reads and writes the same trial history.
- `MlflowSparkStudy` wraps an Optuna `Study` and runs the parallel optimization on PySpark executors.
```
storage = MlflowStorage(experiment_id=exp_id)
study = MlflowSparkStudy(study_name="tune", storage=storage)
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=200, n_jobs=40)
```

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A shared storage backend turns 40 separate searches into one study: each new suggestion by the sampler sees all finished trials, and the result is one set of best parameters. MlflowStorage on the MLflow experiment plus MlflowSparkStudy is the documented way to get it on Spark.
- ✗ **B. Same seed, RandomSampler:** random sampling does not learn from past trials at all, so it gives up the benefit of TPE. Identical seeds would also make the workers repeat the same points instead of covering the space.
- ✗ **C. Merge on the driver afterwards:** merging after the fact gives a table, but the sampler never used the other workers' results while searching. The problem is shared state during the run, not reporting at the end.
- ✗ **D. More trials per worker:** each in-memory study still sees only its own trials, so there are still 40 independent searches. More history per worker costs compute and does not make the workers agree.

## Key idea
Distributed Optuna needs one shared study record: MlflowStorage as the backend and MlflowSparkStudy to run it on executors.
Q011895:
## Two pluggable parts of every Optuna study
- The **sampler** decides which hyperparameters to try next, using the finished trials. Examples are random, grid, TPE and CMA-ES samplers.
- The **pruner** decides whether to stop a running trial early, based on intermediate values the objective reports. Examples are median, successive-halving and hyperband pruners.
## Defaults in MlflowSparkStudy
The Databricks reference for `MlflowSparkStudy` lists the parameters `study_name`, `storage`, `sampler` and `pruner`. It states that `optuna.samplers.TPESampler` is used as the default sampler and `optuna.pruners.MedianPruner` as the default pruner. TPE is a Bayesian method (it models good and bad regions of the space), so it is closer to Hyperopt's `tpe.suggest` than to random search.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Grid sampler and successive halving:** a grid sampler needs an explicit search grid and is never the default, and successive halving is a different pruner that must be passed in.
- ✗ **B. Random search, no pruning:** random sampling is an option you can pass, but it is not the default. A default pruner also exists.
- ✗ **C. CMA-ES and hyperband:** both are valid Optuna components when you pass them yourself, but the documented defaults are TPE and the median pruner.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** TPESampler is the default sampler and MedianPruner is the default pruner, so an unconfigured study already searches with a Bayesian method and can stop trials that look worse than the median of earlier trials at the same step.

## Key idea
MlflowSparkStudy defaults to a TPE sampler and a median pruner; anything else is passed in explicitly.
Q011896:
## Where the integration comes from
`MlflowStorage` and `MlflowSparkStudy` were added with MLflow 3.0. The Databricks Optuna page says MLflow 3.0 is preinstalled on recent Databricks Runtime ML versions, and that on older runtimes you install the latest Optuna and MLflow yourself:
```
%pip install mlflow --upgrade
%pip install optuna
```
## Why a notebook-scoped install is the usual fix
A `%pip` install is notebook-scoped and is distributed to the executors of that session, so parallel trials import the same versions as the driver. Alternatively, choose a runtime that already ships MLflow 3, which keeps a production job reproducible without an install step.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. MlflowStorage only:** the storage class ships in the same MLflow 3 package as the Spark study, so the older MLflow fails on it as well. A plain create_study would also not run on executors.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Upgrading MLflow and installing Optuna in the notebook (or using a newer ML runtime) provides the module that the import needs. This is the exact guidance on the Databricks Optuna page for older runtimes.
- ✗ **C. Hyperopt SparkTrials:** it is a different library and is not a way to run Optuna objectives. Databricks documents it as no longer maintained, so it is not a migration target.
- ✗ **D. Copying package folders:** hand-copied files bypass dependency resolution and do not reach executors reliably. A supported install is both simpler and reproducible.

## Key idea
MlflowStorage and MlflowSparkStudy need MLflow 3: use a runtime that includes it or upgrade MLflow and install Optuna with %pip.
Q011897:
## How pruning works in Optuna
A pruner can only judge a trial by **intermediate values**. The Databricks page documents the pruner as an argument of `MlflowSparkStudy` with `MedianPruner` as the default. A pruner compares what a running trial has reached at a given step with what earlier trials had reached at that step. The objective therefore has to report a value at each epoch (or fold) and end the trial early when the pruner says so, using the pruning interface of the Optuna trial object (see the Optuna documentation).
## Why it matters on Spark
Each trial occupies an executor task. Pruned trials give the slot back quickly, so the same cluster completes many more trials. An objective that returns only one final number gives the pruner nothing to compare, so no trial is ever pruned.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger n_jobs:** n_jobs sets how many trials run at once. It does not let Spark cancel a running function, and it does not produce intermediate values for the pruner.
- ✗ **B. More than 100 trials:** the pruner needs per-step values, not a large trial count. The missing reports are the real cause.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Per-epoch reporting gives the default median pruner the intermediate values it compares, and ending the trial when it signals gives the slot back to a better-chosen trial.
- ✗ **D. SQLite storage:** pruning does not depend on the storage type, and a local file on the driver would not be shared by executors. The change would break the shared study rather than enable pruning.

## Key idea
Pruners act on intermediate values: report them from the training loop and stop the trial when the pruner says so.
Q011898:
## From Hyperopt to Optuna
Hyperopt declares the search space outside the objective (`hp.*` expressions passed to `fmin`) and distributes with `SparkTrials`, which Databricks documents as no longer maintained. Optuna declares the space inside the objective, with `trial.suggest_*` calls, and the Databricks integration distributes it with `MlflowSparkStudy` on `MlflowStorage`.
## The scale of the range
A parameter such as `C` spans many orders of magnitude. A linear draw from `1e-10` to `1e10` puts almost every sample in the top decade. The Databricks Optuna example therefore declares `svr_c = trial.suggest_float('svr_c', 1e-10, 1e10, log=True)`: the bounds are the raw values and `log=True` makes the sampler work on the log scale. Hyperopt's `loguniform` takes the logarithm of the bounds; Optuna does not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Categorical list:** five fixed values throw away the continuous range and give the sampler nothing to model between them. `MlflowSparkStudy` runs a study and is not a sampler.
- ✗ **B. Default linear scale:** Optuna samples linearly unless `log=True` is given, so nearly all trials land in the largest decade.
- ✓ **C. B=Raw bounds with `log=True` plus `MlflowSparkStudy` (correct):** the suggest call keeps the search on a log scale across the 20 orders of magnitude, and the study object replaces `SparkTrials` for parallel execution on executors.
- ✗ **D. Log bounds and SparkTrials:** `SparkTrials` is a Hyperopt class and not an argument of `optuna.create_study`. Log-transformed bounds would also sample between about -23 and 23 as raw values of `C`.

## Key idea
Port Hyperopt log-uniform spaces to Optuna with raw bounds and log=True inside the objective, and SparkTrials to MlflowSparkStudy.
Q011899:
## The cost of fine-grained logging
Every trial writes parameters, intermediate values and a final value. At several hundred concurrent trials this is a large stream of small REST calls to the MLflow tracking server, and a service that throttles will answer with errors or delays, which slows the objective itself.
## Batching in MlflowStorage
The Databricks API reference describes `MlflowStorage` as an MLflow-based storage class for Optuna with batch processing to avoid REST API throttling. Two parameters control it:
- `batch_flush_interval`: seconds between automatic flushes (default 1.0).
- `batch_size_threshold`: maximum number of items collected before a flush is triggered (default 100).
Because the storage is also what Optuna reads for the shared study, it serves both as logging and as coordination for the samplers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Logging only a sample:** sampling would drop trials from the study history, which harms the sampler. All trials are recorded.
- ✗ **B. One write after the last trial:** nothing could then be shared during the search, so TPE would not see other workers' results, and a driver failure would lose all trials. The flush happens during the run.
- ✗ **C. Delta table instead of tracking server:** the storage is based on the MLflow experiment, so it still talks to the tracking server. It reduces the call rate by batching, not by changing the backend.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** MlflowStorage collects writes in a batch and flushes on an interval or when the batch reaches a size threshold. That reduces the number of REST calls and avoids throttling, while still keeping the whole shared study in the experiment.

## Key idea
MlflowStorage batches Optuna writes (flush interval and size threshold) to avoid MLflow REST throttling at high concurrency.
Q011900:
## Ray on Spark
Ray on Databricks creates a Ray cluster **on top of a Spark cluster**: `ray.util.spark.setup_ray_cluster` starts a background Spark job, each Spark task becomes a Ray worker node, and the Ray head runs on the Spark driver. Because it needs this kind of cluster, the documentation lists limits:
- Ray on Spark is supported for **dedicated** access mode, **no isolation shared** access mode and **jobs clusters** only.
- A Ray cluster created with the Ray-on-Spark integration cannot be started on serverless-based runtimes. For serverless GPU compute there is a separate offering, Ray on AI Runtime.
## Decision
For a CPU Ray Tune workload, use an ML runtime cluster in a supported access mode (or a jobs cluster for scheduled runs).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. autoscale flag:** autoscaling only changes how many Ray workers exist on a cluster that already supports Ray on Spark. It cannot make serverless compute a valid host.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Dedicated or no-isolation shared access mode, or a jobs cluster, are the supported places to create a Ray-on-Spark cluster. Serverless compute is not, so the work moves to a supported cluster.
- ✗ **C. Standard shared access mode:** the documented supported modes are dedicated and no isolation shared, so standard shared mode is not one of them. No container-isolated Ray worker exists in this integration.
- ✗ **D. pip install on serverless:** Ray being installed does not help, because the limitation lies in the compute type, not in the package. The integration depends on a Spark cluster to place Ray worker nodes.

## Key idea
Ray on Spark needs dedicated or no-isolation shared access mode or a jobs cluster; serverless GPU work uses Ray on AI Runtime.
Q011901:
## Per-user and global Ray clusters
- `setup_ray_cluster` creates a Ray cluster that is **only available to the notebook user** who created it. It is shut down automatically after the notebook is detached or after 30 minutes without submitted tasks.
- `setup_global_ray_cluster` (Ray 2.9.0 and above) creates a **global mode** cluster that all users attached to the Databricks compute can use. It has no inactivity timeout: it runs until the blocking call is interrupted or the cluster stops.
## Properties of global mode
- Only one active global mode Ray cluster per Databricks cluster.
- Any attached notebook can call `ray.init()` to connect.
- Because many users share it, resource contention can occur, so size it and schedule heavy runs with care.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A global mode Ray cluster, started from a notebook job and kept running, is the documented way to share one Ray cluster among users independent of any single notebook.
- ✗ **B. Each analyst runs setup_ray_cluster:** every call makes a separate, user-specific Ray cluster, not a shared one. Costs multiply and nothing is shared.
- ✗ **C. Head on a laptop:** the Ray cluster CLI is not supported on Databricks, and the Job CLI is for submitting jobs from outside through the driver proxy. It does not turn a laptop into the head of a cluster.
- ✗ **D. Longer idle timeout:** the 30-minute inactivity limit is not what removes the cluster here, since detaching the notebook shuts it down too. A per-user cluster stays tied to the notebook.

## Key idea
Use setup_global_ray_cluster for a shared, notebook-independent Ray cluster; setup_ray_cluster is per user and stops on detach.
Q011902:
## Why `%pip` stops Ray
A `%pip` command restarts the Python process of the notebook environment. The Ray cluster was started from that process as a background Spark job, so the restart tears it down. The Ray on Databricks page says to avoid `%pip` on a running Ray cluster for this reason, and to install libraries before initializing it.
## Practical order
1. Install notebook-scoped libraries (`%pip`) or use cluster libraries.
2. Call `setup_ray_cluster` and `ray.init()`.
3. Run Tune or other Ray workloads.
Related guidance: with Ray 2.12 and above, remote Ray tasks can use notebook-scoped and cluster Python libraries; on Ray 2.11 and below, dependencies must be pre-installed in the session with `%pip` before starting the cluster.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. A second notebook:** a separate notebook's %pip may leave your Ray cluster alone, but the libraries are then not installed in the session that runs the new experiment, and the problem recurs when you install there.
- ✗ **B. Subprocess pip inside trials:** this installs on whichever worker runs the trial each time, adds start-up delay to every trial and gives no consistent environment. It is not the documented approach.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Installing before the Ray cluster is initialized keeps the cluster from being stopped, and the Ray tasks then see the libraries as well.
- ✗ **D. ray.shutdown() around pip:** a client disconnect does not protect a cluster that lives in the notebook process. The cluster is lost anyway, and the documented fix is the order of operations.

## Key idea
Do not %pip install on a live Ray cluster; install libraries first, then create the Ray cluster.
Q011903:
## Why Ray tasks need explicit credentials
Ray tasks run in separate worker processes started by the Ray-on-Spark cluster. They do not inherit the interactive notebook's authentication context, so MLflow calls from inside a task cannot authenticate by themselves.
## The documented setup
The Ray on Databricks page ("Using MLflow in Ray tuner, Ray train or customized Ray tasks") says integration requires Ray 2.41 or above, and that you set environment variables **before** calling `ray.util.spark.setup_ray_cluster`:
```
os.environ["DATABRICKS_HOST"] = "https://<workspace>"
os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"] = "<secret>"
setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=2, min_worker_nodes=2)
```
Alternatively use `DATABRICKS_HOST` with `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` and `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET` (a service principal). Read secrets from a secret scope rather than typing them into a notebook.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Head node only:** restricting the job to the head would remove the distributed trials, and on Databricks the Ray head has 0 CPUs by default. Remote tasks may call MLflow once they have credentials.
- ✗ **B. Token in tune.report:** a metric report is not an authentication channel, and putting a token in each report would expose the secret in results.
- ✗ **C. mlflow.autolog on the driver:** autologging configures the driver session and does not transfer credentials to separate Ray worker processes.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Environment variables for host and credentials, set before the Ray cluster is created, are passed to the Ray workers, so the tasks can talk to the tracking server.

## Key idea
Set DATABRICKS_HOST and credentials as environment variables before setup_ray_cluster so Ray tasks can log to MLflow.
Q011904:
## Hybrid Spark and Ray
Ray on Databricks runs inside a Spark cluster. Both frameworks want the same machines: Spark executors use JVM heap and cache memory, Ray workers use Python heap and an object store. The scaling page gives two rules for hybrid workloads:
- **Compute**: with a fixed number of nodes, enable Ray-on-Spark autoscaling. When no Ray work is running, the Ray cluster scales down and the nodes are free for Spark tasks; when Ray is used again, it scales up. Use `min_worker_nodes` and `max_worker_nodes` (Ray 2.10 and above); scale-down speed can be tuned with `autoscale_idle_timeout_minutes`.
- **Memory**: reduce `spark.executor.memory` to a small value (the docs give 4g as an example), because the Spark executor holds dataset caches and triggers garbage collection lazily, which takes memory away from Ray and can cause out-of-memory errors.
You can also make the Databricks cluster itself autoscale and cap Ray at a subset, for example Ray on at most 4 of up to 10 nodes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Autoscaling the Ray-on-Spark cluster lets idle Ray workers go away so Spark tasks can use the nodes, and a small executor memory leaves room for Ray. This is the documented hybrid configuration.
- ✗ **B. Maximum executor memory:** large executor heaps make the competition worse because Ray's heap and object store are then starved. The docs recommend the opposite.
- ✗ **C. One Ray worker all day:** the two frameworks do share a cluster by design, and a single worker would remove the parallelism the search needs.
- ✗ **D. A Ray cluster per Spark task:** a global cluster is one per Databricks cluster and is for sharing among users. More heads would multiply the head overhead and not release workers to Spark.

## Key idea
For hybrid Spark and Ray, autoscale the Ray cluster so idle workers return to Spark, and keep spark.executor.memory small.
Q011905:
## GPU slots are a Spark resource too
On a GPU cluster, Spark can schedule tasks by GPU: each task requests `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` GPUs. If that is 1, a Spark task needs a GPU to run, so the number of concurrent tasks is capped by the (few) GPUs and GPU-hungry Ray workloads are blocked while Spark runs.
## The recommendation
The Ray on Databricks create page ("Non-GPU workloads") describes a typical flow: Spark with UDFs for simple preprocessing that needs no GPUs, then Ray for complex ML that does. It recommends setting `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` to `0` at the Spark cluster level. The benefits stated are:
- Higher Spark parallelism, because a GPU instance usually has many more CPU cores than GPU devices.
- On a shared cluster, Spark jobs do not compete for GPUs with concurrently running Ray workloads.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zero head node resources:** the Ray head already defaults to 0 CPUs and 0 GPUs on Databricks, so this changes nothing about GPU contention from Spark tasks.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Setting the GPU amount per Spark task to 0 lets DataFrame transformations run on all CPU cores without claiming GPUs, so Ray keeps the GPUs and Spark gets more parallelism.
- ✗ **C. All GPUs to each Spark task:** it would make Spark reserve even more GPUs per task, so fewer Spark tasks run and Ray has no GPUs left.
- ✗ **D. Full executor memory:** it does not stop Spark tasks from requesting GPUs, and a very large executor heap reduces what is left for Ray.

## Key idea
For Spark preprocessing before GPU Ray training, set spark.task.resource.gpu.amount to 0.
Q011906:
## Scale up first, then out
**Vertical scaling** means a bigger machine (more memory, cores or GPUs). **Horizontal scaling** means more machines. For deep learning the Databricks "Distributed training" page says: when possible, train neural networks on a single machine, because distributed code for training and inference is more complex than single-machine code and slower due to communication overhead. Consider distributed training and inference when the model or the data are too large to fit in memory on a single machine.
## The cost of going out
Synchronous distributed training exchanges gradients between processes every step. Over a network that takes time that a single machine with fast links (or one GPU) never spends. The compute saved is only worth the overhead when a single machine cannot hold the work.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CPU cluster:** Databricks Runtime ML includes TorchDistributor, the DeepSpeed distributor and Ray for GPU clusters, so GPUs and distributed training can be combined. CPU nodes would also train a network much more slowly.
- ✗ **B. Always distribute:** the documentation says the opposite, because of code complexity and communication overhead.
- ✗ **C. Convert to Spark ML:** Spark ML trains classical algorithms on DataFrames; a PyTorch network is not converted into a Spark ML pipeline by a flag.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The documentation prefers one machine and distributes only when the model or data exceed memory. Here both fit, so a bigger single instance is the cheapest path.

## Key idea
Prefer one machine for neural networks; scale out only when the model or data exceed single-machine memory.
Q011907:
## Distributed Spark ML from a client
Spark ML algorithms train over partitioned DataFrames, so memory and compute grow with the cluster. The Databricks "Distributed training" page says Databricks offers distributed training for Spark ML models with the `pyspark.ml.connect` module, to train Spark ML models and run model inference. In Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above, Spark ML is enabled by default in Standard compute, so you can use Spark's distributed machine learning without managing a full cluster.
## What the other tools are for
- `TorchDistributor`, the DeepSpeed distributor and Ray are listed for deep learning and custom parallel code.
- Plain scikit-learn runs in one Python process: after `toPandas()` it runs in the IDE process, on the local machine.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. TorchDistributor:** it launches PyTorch training code, not Spark ML algorithms.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** pyspark.ml.connect is the documented route for distributed Spark ML training and inference on Standard compute with Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above, so the data stays on the cluster.
- ✗ **C. toPandas then scikit-learn:** `toPandas()` pulls all rows into the client process, which is too small for the data, and a scikit-learn fit runs in that one process and is never sent to the cluster.
- ✗ **D. Global Ray cluster:** Ray on Spark is documented for dedicated access mode, no isolation shared access mode and jobs clusters, not for Standard compute, and Ray is not the Spark ML route.

## Key idea
For classical Spark ML at scale from a client, use pyspark.ml.connect on Standard compute (Databricks Runtime 17.0 and above).
Q011908:
## Where the error comes from
Synchronous distributed training exchanges gradients between processes through a communication library. On GPUs this is NCCL (backend `nccl`); on CPU instances it is Gloo (backend `gloo`). Both the TorchDistributor page and the Ray on Databricks page list the same multi-node symptom: `ncclInternalError: Internal check failed` means NCCL cannot use some of the network interfaces for GPU communication.
## Documented fixes by symptom
- `ncclInternalError: Internal check failed`: set `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` to `eth0` in the training code (primary network interface).
- `peer access is not supported between these two devices` (on G5 GPUs on AWS): set `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE` to `1`.
- Gloo `RuntimeError: Connection refused` on CPU instances: set `GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME` to `eth0`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Gloo on GPUs:** gloo appears in the documentation as the CPU backend, with its own interface variable, not as a replacement for NCCL on GPU clusters.
- ✗ **B. NCCL_P2P_DISABLE:** the documented use is the different error about peer access between two devices on G5 GPUs. It does not select the network interface between nodes.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Pointing NCCL at the primary network interface with NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME is the documented remedy for this multi-node error.
- ✗ **D. More processes:** extra processes do not change which interface NCCL uses, and a process count above the GPU count is not how NCCL selects a network path.

## Key idea
ncclInternalError on multi-node GPU training: set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to eth0 so NCCL uses the primary network interface.
Q011909:
## Diminishing returns in synchronous training
In data-parallel training each step ends with a gradient exchange between all processes. The compute per step shrinks when the batch is split across more processes, but the exchange time stays or grows with node count and network latency. Past a point, extra nodes mostly wait.
## What to do
- Stay on the smallest number of machines that meets the time target; the Databricks "Distributed training" page notes that distributed code can be slower because of communication overhead.
- Use machines with more GPUs per node (fast links inside a node) rather than more single-GPU nodes.
- Increase the per-GPU batch size so compute per step grows relative to the exchange.
These choices reduce the share of time spent in communication.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The signature of communication overhead is a falling GPU utilization and diminishing speed-up as nodes are added. Consolidating onto fewer or larger machines is the fitting response when the model fits.
- ✗ **B. GPU amount per Spark task:** that setting is about Spark tasks claiming GPUs in mixed Spark and Ray flows. It does not change the gradient exchange of a training job already running.
- ✗ **C. Smaller model and CPUs:** the 6x speed-up at 8 nodes shows that the GPUs were useful. CPUs would make training slower overall.
- ✗ **D. Autoscaling down:** an autoscale removal during training would fail or stall the job rather than produce steady diminishing returns at higher node counts.

## Key idea
Diminishing speed-up with falling GPU utilization signals communication overhead: prefer fewer, larger machines.
Q011910:
## Ray workers get only what you declare
`setup_ray_cluster` starts a background Spark job, and each Spark task becomes a Ray worker node. The Databricks scaling page gives the defaults for a Ray worker node: `num_cpus_worker_node` is 1 and `num_gpus_worker_node` is 0. A Ray worker that declares zero GPUs can never run a task that requests a GPU, whatever hardware the Spark worker has.
## Recommended sizing
Set `num_cpus_worker_node` to the number of CPU cores per Spark worker and `num_gpus_worker_node` to the number of GPUs per Spark worker. Then each Spark worker launches one Ray worker node that fully uses the machine.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Declaring the cores and GPUs per Ray worker node lets the Ray scheduler place GPU trials on them, and one Ray worker per Spark worker uses the whole node.
- ✗ **B. GPUs on the head:** the head runs on the Spark driver and by default has 0 CPUs and 0 GPUs; GPU capacity for trials comes from the Ray worker nodes.
- ✗ **C. Small executor memory:** this setting is recommended for hybrid Spark and Ray memory pressure and does not declare GPUs to Ray.
- ✗ **D. 24 Ray workers:** each would still declare 0 GPUs by default, so GPU trials still could not be placed.

## Key idea
Ray workers default to 1 CPU and 0 GPUs: set num_cpus_worker_node and num_gpus_worker_node to the per-node hardware.
Q011911:
## Planning for growth
Scaling up is simple: same code, bigger instance. Its limits are (1) a maximum instance size, (2) rising cost per unit of memory at the top end, and (3) a single point of failure. Scaling out adds machines, which in data-parallel algorithms means more partitions and more memory; the limits are later but the price is complexity and communication.
## Trade-off to state
- Choose a single node while the data fits with margin; it is simpler, usually faster for small data and easier to debug.
- Plan the move to a distributed implementation when the growth curve will pass the largest node, because rewriting a pipeline under pressure is costly. Check that the algorithm exists in Spark ML and validate that its quality matches.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No validation needed:** partitioning does not prevent overfitting, and the Spark ML model needs the same evaluation as any other.
- ✗ **B. MLflow only for distributed jobs:** MLflow tracks runs from single-node code equally well.
- ✓ **C. The real reason to plan ahead is the ceiling (correct):** growth will pass any single machine, and Spark ML's data parallelism continues to scale with workers. The overhead is the price, so it is a trade-off, not a free win.
- ✗ **D. Always faster:** for data that fits on a node the communication and scheduling overhead often make the distributed version slower, so the claim is false.

## Key idea
Scale up while data fits; plan to scale out before data growth passes the largest node, accepting communication overhead.
Q011912:
## Data parallelism versus model parallelism
- **Data parallelism**: every process keeps a complete copy of the model. The dataset is divided into shards, each process computes gradients for its shard, and the gradients are averaged (all-reduce) so the copies stay identical. It speeds up training when the model fits in one device but the data (or the number of steps) is large.
- **Model parallelism** (including pipeline parallelism): the model itself is split across devices because it does not fit in one. It is a memory solution, not a throughput one.
## On Databricks
`TorchDistributor` (a PySpark module in Databricks Runtime ML) launches PyTorch training as a Spark job, initializes the communication channels and uses `torch.distributed.run`. A typical function uses `DistributedDataParallel` and a `DistributedSampler` and is run with `TorchDistributor(num_processes=..., local_mode=False, use_gpu=True).run(train, ...)`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bigger driver:** training runs in the worker processes, and a larger driver does not speed up epochs.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The model fits on one GPU and the problem is data volume, so data parallelism is the match. TorchDistributor runs DDP across the GPU workers, each with its own shard.
- ✗ **C. Model parallelism:** it is used when the model does not fit in one GPU. This model fits, so splitting layers adds pipeline waiting without addressing the data volume.
- ✗ **D. Different learning rates per GPU:** that is a hyperparameter search, which finds a setting but does not shorten the time to pass over the data for a given model.

## Key idea
Model fits and data is large: data parallelism (full model copies on shards, gradients synchronized), for example with TorchDistributor.
Q011913:
## When replicas do not fit
Plain data parallelism copies the whole model (weights, gradients and optimizer states) to every GPU. If one copy does not fit in a GPU, adding replicas only adds more failures. The memory has to be partitioned or the model split across devices.
## Databricks guidance
The "Distributed training with DeepSpeed distributor" page says it is built on top of TorchDistributor and is the recommended solution for customers with models that require higher compute power but are limited by memory constraints. DeepSpeed (open source, from Microsoft) offers optimized memory usage, reduced communication overhead and advanced pipeline parallelism. The page lists low GPU memory, large model training and large input data such as batch inference as scenarios. An example notebook fine-tunes a 7B chat model with it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Doubling num_processes:** each process still builds a complete replica, so there is no halving of a model. More processes mean more copies and the same out-of-memory error.
- ✗ **B. Ray Tune:** Ray Tune runs hyperparameter trials. It does not partition a model across GPUs.
- ✗ **C. Spark ML estimators:** pyspark.ml covers classical algorithms and does not shard weights of PyTorch language models.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The DeepSpeed distributor targets this exact case, models that are limited by GPU memory, with memory optimizations and pipeline parallelism on top of TorchDistributor.

## Key idea
Model too big for one GPU: use memory-saving, model-splitting tools such as the DeepSpeed distributor, not more full replicas.
Q011914:
## How the training function reaches the workers
`TorchDistributor.run(main, *args)` calls `main(**kwargs)` for a function (or runs `torchrun` for a file path). A function defined in a notebook is serialized on the driver and sent to the executors, where each process starts its own Python interpreter. References to modules imported at notebook level, to open handles or to stateful objects often do not survive that transfer.
## Documented guidance
The TorchDistributor page lists a common notebook error where objects cannot be found or pickled because import statements were not distributed to the executors. The fix is to include all imports at the top of the function passed to `run`, and inside any other user-defined function that the training method calls. It also suggests keeping the whole distributed logic inside one training function and reading `device_id` from `LOCAL_RANK`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. local_mode=True:** it changes where the processes run, not how the function is shipped. Moving the same function with outside imports gives the same type of error.
- ✗ **B. Lambda:** serialization of a lambda has more restrictions than a named function, and it would hide the import problem rather than fix it.
- ✗ **C. Broadcast a module:** Python modules are not data to broadcast, and the problem is the serialization of references, which broadcasting does not repair.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Imports inside the training function and its helpers run in each worker process, so no module object has to be pickled from the driver.

## Key idea
With TorchDistributor, put imports inside the training function and any helpers it calls so workers resolve them locally.
Q011915:
## What DDP does and does not do
`DistributedDataParallel` replicates the model per process and synchronizes **gradients**. It does not shard the data. Each process builds its own `DataLoader`, so without a distributed sampler all processes iterate over the full dataset. The work is repeated 4 times and the gradients are averaged over nearly identical batches.
## Sharding the data
`torch.utils.data.DistributedSampler` divides the dataset indices among the processes by rank, so each process reads about one quarter of the data per epoch. The Databricks TorchDistributor example does exactly this: it builds `DDP(model)`, `DistributedSampler(dataset)` and `DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler)` inside the training function.
```
sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler, batch_size=64)
```

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A distributed sampler splits each epoch's samples across the processes, which is what makes the data-parallel step faster. Gradient synchronization by DDP is then useful because each process sees different data.
- ✗ **B. Whole-dataset batch:** it would exceed GPU memory, and each process would still read all samples.
- ✗ **C. DataParallel on the driver:** it is the older single-process, multi-GPU approach, not a way to split data across Spark workers, and TorchDistributor is set up for DDP.
- ✗ **D. GPU amount per Spark task:** this setting is about Spark tasks and GPU claims, and does not control how a PyTorch loader selects samples.

## Key idea
DDP only synchronizes gradients: add a DistributedSampler so each process trains on its own shard.
Q011916:
## Two levels of parallelism share one budget
Hyperparameter tuning is parallel across trials and each trial may be parallel within itself (data parallelism). Both draw from the same GPU pool, so the split is a trade-off.
- Trial-level parallelism has almost no communication cost, because trials are independent.
- Data parallelism inside a trial has a synchronization cost that grows with the number of processes (see the Databricks distributed training page about communication overhead).
## Reasoning
If a trial scales well to 8 GPUs but poorly to 64, spend the budget on 64 / 8 = 8 concurrent trials: the 40 trials then need 5 waves. Running one trial on 64 GPUs wastes capacity on diminishing returns. Trial-level concurrency is also where Optuna and Ray Tune help, by allocating resources per trial. The per-trial size depends on the measured scaling curve and the model memory, not on a rule.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One trial at a time on 64 GPUs:** communication overhead grows with process count, so gains from 8 to 64 GPUs are usually small. That leaves trials waiting in a queue.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Eight concurrent trials of 8 GPUs each keep every GPU busy and avoid the large synchronization cost of a 64-process job, so the 40 trials finish in about five waves.
- ✗ **C. Fractional GPUs:** a model that needs 8 GPUs for data parallelism cannot be given 1.6 GPUs without changing the design, and 40 simultaneous trials would not fit.
- ✗ **D. Single-GPU trials:** the statement is not generally true. If one GPU cannot hold the data volume or the time per trial grows too much, the data parallelism inside the trial pays for itself.

## Key idea
Split the GPU budget between concurrent trials and the width of each trial using the measured scaling curve; avoid wide jobs with poor scaling.
Q011917:
## Match the framework to the model family
- **Spark ML** (`pyspark.ml`) implements classical algorithms (linear and logistic regression, tree ensembles, k-means and others) over DataFrames, with data parallelism built into the algorithms. Databricks also offers `pyspark.ml.connect` for distributed training and inference of Spark ML models from Databricks Connect.
- **TorchDistributor, DeepSpeed distributor and Ray** are the options listed on the Distributed training page for deep learning workloads, where the training code is PyTorch (or Ray Train) code that you write.
## Decision
A 2 TB table with a tree ensemble and a linear model is a Spark ML case: the algorithm reads partitioned DataFrame data, and nothing needs rewriting as a PyTorch training loop. TorchDistributor is for launching distributed PyTorch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Sampling is the only way:** distributed algorithms for tabular data exist, with Spark ML as the main example, so sampling is a choice and not a necessity.
- ✗ **B. local_mode=True:** local mode is not a data-distribution switch, and a 2 TB table is not spread automatically by it. The decision between frameworks is the question.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Spark ML estimators are built for partitioned DataFrames, so they train classical models on data that exceeds one node. TorchDistributor serves PyTorch code and is not the route for these models.
- ✗ **D. Wrapping scikit-learn in PyTorch:** TorchDistributor launches PyTorch processes. A scikit-learn estimator wrapped in a module is still trained on one process' data, and not distributed.

## Key idea
Classical models on data too big for one node: Spark ML; TorchDistributor, DeepSpeed and Ray are for custom (deep learning) training code.
